article_title: Bilingual Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition (BCIRC) (English Language Learners)
citation: Bilingual Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition. (2007). WWC Intervention Report. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED405428
title: BCIRC before-, during-, and after-reading activity structure
description: BCIRC organizes instruction as a recurring cycle of fifteen activities occurring before, during, and after reading. As the report describes, "Fifteen activities occur before, during, and after reading, including using BCIRC materials to develop vocabulary, making predictions of a story's content based on its title, and reading with a partner followed by silent reading". Teachers model reading strategies such as making and confirming a prediction before, during, and after reading, and cooperative groups then apply the demonstrated strategy while attempting to comprehend stories from their classroom text. The pattern embeds vocabulary, prediction, partner reading, and writing within cooperative teams.
requirements: Teachers combine CIRC strategies with transitional and English as a Second Language strategies
Extensive staff development on facilitating cooperative learning discussions
constraints: Designed for students transitioning from Spanish primary-language reading instruction in grades 2-5
target_learners: Elementary English language learners whose primary home language is Spanish
target_learning_goals: Cooperative discussion and academic English use
examples: In the reviewed study, teachers modeled strategies such as making and confirming a prediction, and cooperative groups then applied the demonstrated strategy while attempting to comprehend stories selected from their classroom text
key_sources: Bilingual Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition. (2007). WWC Intervention Report. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED405428

article_title: Causal Modelling of Support Interventions for Student Competency Assessment
citation: Francesca Mangili, Alessandro Antonucci, Rafael Cabañas de Paz. (2026). Causal Modelling of Support Interventions for Student Competency Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24632
title: bcause open-source software for causal inference in Bayesian and credal networks
description: The bcause open-source software was used to compute all group and individual inferences in the article's use case. As the article notes, "All inferences were computed using thebcause open-source software", available at github.com/PGM-Lab/bcause. It supports the causal EM back-propagation procedure and the interventional and counterfactual queries of the proposed protocol.
requirements: The current software implementation supports only exact BN inference
constraints: Exact inference may hinder application to case studies involving many skills when questions induce strong relations among them; supporting approximate BN inference is stated as necessary future work
examples: Used to compute the five-fold cross-validation comparison, group marginals, PN/PS probabilities and individual counterfactuals in the CAT use case
key_sources: Francesca Mangili, Alessandro Antonucci, Rafael Cabañas de Paz. (2026). Causal Modelling of Support Interventions for Student Competency Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24632

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: Brain-compatible e-learning intervention for Technical Programming 1 (Moodle lessons with interactive sorting and fizzbuzz tasks)
description: The intervention is an e-learning package delivered via Moodle lessons augmenting lectures, containing an "Interactive sorting algorithm presentation", an "Interactive question during fizzbuzz code execution", and "Example of immediate interactive feedback during fizzbuzz task" (Figures 3.4-3.6). It "incorporated several brain-compatible learning principles" and was "administered as a controlled experiment intervention" to a sample group whose performance was compared to a control group of the rest of the class.
requirements: Material must be designed according to sound pedagogical principles to be effective in blended learning
constraints: Designed to augment, not replace, the lecturer's function
target_learners: second-year National Diploma: Software Development students in Technical Programming 1
target_learning_goals: problem-solving strategies and algorithm design skills
key_sources: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.09.008

article_title: A Benefit-Cost Analysis of a Long-Term Intervention on Social and Emotional Learning in Compulsory School
citation: Alli Klapp, Clive Belfield, Brooks Bowden, Henry Levin, Robert Shand, Sabine Zander. (2017). A benefit-cost analysis of a long-term intervention on social and emotional learning in compulsory school. International Journal of Emotional Education, 9(1), 3-19. https://www.um.edu.mt/ijee
title: Benefit-cost analysis framework for SEL interventions
description: The article outlines a benefit-cost analysis framework for SEL interventions in which costs and benefits are compared in monetary values to derive a net present value. Costs are estimated with "the ingredients method (Levin & McEwan, 2001)", where each component of the intervention is investigated in detail. Benefits require linking a measured SE competence to a later outcome with a shadow price; the framework explicitly addresses temporal dynamics — the "ratchet effect" (how fast benefits occur) and the "fade-out effect" (how long they last) — and general spill-over effects on the school, which "should be addressed when calculating the benefits of an intervention".
requirements: A measurement of a specific SE competence that can be linked to a later outcome such as less drug use, plus a monetary shadow price for that outcome
Detailed documentation of intervention resources and costs, since no standardized cost-calculation procedure exists for SEL evaluations
constraints: Long-term adult outcomes usually cannot be followed experimentally for SEL interventions, so informed projections must be used; ratchet and fade-out effects are hard to identify from current evidence
Shadow prices based on cost-of-illness or defensive expenditures are conservative and may understate the true burden
target_learners: students in kindergarten and compulsory schooling receiving universal SEL interventions
target_learning_goals: social and emotional competencies with monetizable downstream outcomes such as reduced drug use
examples: The framework was applied to the Swedish SET intervention, comparing intervention costs against treatment impact on self-reported drug use with sensitivity analyses
key_sources: Alli Klapp, Clive Belfield, Brooks Bowden, Henry Levin, Robert Shand, Sabine Zander. (2017). A benefit-cost analysis of a long-term intervention on social and emotional learning in compulsory school. International Journal of Emotional Education, 9(1), 3-19. https://www.um.edu.mt/ijee

article_title: Between-Case Standardized Mean Differences: Flexible Methods for Single-Case Designs
citation: Man Chen, James E. Pustejovsky, David A. Klingbeil, and Ethan R. Van Norman. (2023). Between-Case Standardized Mean Differences: Flexible Methods for Single-Case Designs. Journal of School Psychology, vol. 98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2023.02.002
title: BC-SMD framework: a hierarchical-model-based, design-comparable effect size for single-case designs
description: The BC-SMD is an effect size metric for single-case designs defined by first fitting a hierarchical linear model to the SCD data, then using it to consider a hypothetical between-group design with the same population, intervention, and outcome. The article states it is "theoretically comparable to a standardized mean difference from a between-group design performed with the same population, the same intervention, and the same outcome measures." The framework models within-case and between-case variation and standardizes the treatment-phase mean difference by total variance, putting results on the between-group SMD metric so SCD evidence can enter meta-analyses and evidence-based practice reviews.
requirements: Replication across participants is required so that between-participant variation in the outcome can be estimated and comparability with between-group effect sizes achieved
A well-specified model for the single-case data, chosen using theory, visual analysis, and preliminary model-comparison analyses
constraints: Initial developments assumed stable baselines without trends, no treatment-phase trends, and homogeneous treatment effects; the later HLM framework relaxes these
To date BC-SMD methods had only been formally developed for two types of SCDs, which the What Works Clearinghouse's adoption has been criticized for
target_learners: students receiving academic and behavioral interventions studied via single-case designs
target_learning_goals: quantifying and synthesizing magnitudes of academic and behavioral intervention effects
examples: Applied in meta-analyses of single-case research and adopted by the What Works Clearinghouse as a metric for summarizing SCD findings
key_sources: Man Chen, James E. Pustejovsky, David A. Klingbeil, and Ethan R. Van Norman. (2023). Between-Case Standardized Mean Differences: Flexible Methods for Single-Case Designs. Journal of School Psychology, vol. 98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2023.02.002

article_title: Psychotherapeutic Competencies in Blended Care Psychotherapy: Development of a Competence Framework.
citation: Weiher Gerald Marc, Woide Mirjam Naomi, Zirenko Maria, Tremmel Michael, Stangier Ulrich, Horz Holger. (2026). Psychotherapeutic Competencies in Blended Care Psychotherapy: Development of a Competence Framework. JMIR Mental Health. https://doi.org/10.2196/100125
title: The BCP Competence Framework: 8 Competence Domains, Modalities, and Competence Facets
description: The article introduces a theoretically grounded framework of psychotherapeutic competencies for blended care psychotherapy. It organizes competencies around Modalities of BCP (eg, face-to-face, videoconferencing, and apps), Competence Facets (knowledge, skills, and attitudes), and 8 Competence Domains including Creation of Setting and Infrastructure, Transfer of Communication and Methods, Therapeutic Relationship, Self-Regulation Self-Confidence and Self-Care, Data Security Legal Issues Ethics and Safety, Technological Aspects, Scientific Knowledge and Methods, and Individual and Cultural Diversity. The framework was developed in four steps, integrating educational and clinical psychology competence models, an expert workshop, and a systematic review of 35 studies.
requirements: Developed through a four-step process including an exploratory literature search, a preliminary theoretical framework, an expert workshop with 5 licensed psychotherapists, and integration of a systematic review of 35 studies
constraints: The framework is theoretically grounded and evidence-informed but not yet externally or empirically validated
target_learning_goals: competencies required for effective delivery of blended care psychotherapy
key_sources: Weiher Gerald Marc, Woide Mirjam Naomi, Zirenko Maria, Tremmel Michael, Stangier Ulrich, Horz Holger. (2026). Psychotherapeutic Competencies in Blended Care Psychotherapy: Development of a Competence Framework. JMIR Mental Health. https://doi.org/10.2196/100125

article_title: Psychotherapeutic Competencies in Blended Care Psychotherapy: Development of a Competence Framework.
citation: Weiher Gerald Marc, Woide Mirjam Naomi, Zirenko Maria, Tremmel Michael, Stangier Ulrich, Horz Holger. (2026). Psychotherapeutic Competencies in Blended Care Psychotherapy: Development of a Competence Framework. JMIR Mental Health. https://doi.org/10.2196/100125
title: Competence Domains clustered into 3 overarching thematic areas: Foundational, Psychotherapeutic Process, and Reflexive
description: The article organizes the 8 Competence Domains into 3 overarching thematic clusters. The Foundational Cluster contains Data Security Legal Issues Ethics and Safety, Technological Aspects, and Creation of Setting and Infrastructure, providing structural, technical, and legal conditions necessary for BCP. The Psychotherapeutic Process Cluster encompasses Therapeutic Relationship and Transfer of Communication and Methods. The Reflexive Cluster incorporates Self-Regulation Self-Confidence and Self-Care along with Individual and Cultural Diversity and Scientific Knowledge and Methods.
requirements: Consistent with the approach used in the systematic review, with the 2 additional competence domains drawn from Rodolfa et al integrated
constraints: The Reflexive Cluster extends previous existing competence frameworks in digital contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding the thematic organization of BCP competencies
key_sources: Weiher Gerald Marc, Woide Mirjam Naomi, Zirenko Maria, Tremmel Michael, Stangier Ulrich, Horz Holger. (2026). Psychotherapeutic Competencies in Blended Care Psychotherapy: Development of a Competence Framework. JMIR Mental Health. https://doi.org/10.2196/100125

article_title: The effects of personalized video feedback of basic cardiac life support on knowledge and skills levels in undergraduate nursing students: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Mohsenzadeh Habibeh, Farsi Zahra, Afaghi Effat. (2025). The effects of personalized video feedback of basic cardiac life support on knowledge and skills levels in undergraduate nursing students: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06935-z
title: BCLS knowledge questionnaire and BCLS skills checklist
description: Two measurement instruments used to assess outcomes in the trial. The knowledge questionnaire contains 20 four-choice items scored 0–20 (low = 0–9, moderate = 10–15, high = 16–20), and the skills checklist "consisted of 30 items to measure BCLS skills" scored dichotomously over a 0–30 range (low = 0–9, moderate = 10–20, high = 21–30). Both were updated based on the 2020 American Heart Association Guidelines for CPCR and their validity and reliability were reconfirmed in this study.
requirements: Face validity checked with 20 fourth-year nursing students and content validity confirmed by 10 academic staff members in critical care nursing.
constraints: In this study the knowledge questionnaire's Cronbach's alpha was 0.64 and test-retest r = 0.89; the skills checklist interrater kappa was 91%.
examples: The BCLS knowledge questionnaire classifies knowledge as low = 0–9, moderate = 10–15, and high = 16–20.
key_sources: Mohsenzadeh Habibeh, Farsi Zahra, Afaghi Effat. (2025). The effects of personalized video feedback of basic cardiac life support on knowledge and skills levels in undergraduate nursing students: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06935-z

article_title: Theory-based electronic learning intervention to support appropriate antibiotic prescribing by nurse and pharmacist independent prescribers: an acceptability and feasibility experimental study using mixed methods.
citation: Lim Rosemary, Courtenay Molly, Deslandes Rhian, Ferriday Rebecca, Gillespie David, Hodson Karen, Reid Nicholas, Thomas Neil, Chater Angel. (2020). Theory-based electronic learning intervention to support appropriate antibiotic prescribing by nurse and pharmacist independent prescribers: an acceptability and feasibility experimental study using mixed methods. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-036181
title: Behaviour change wheel with COM-B and Theoretical Domains Framework as intervention design method
description: The intervention was designed using "The behaviour change wheel (BCW) three-stage, eight-step approach", using the COM-B model "to create a behavioural diagnosis that is, what needs to change" and the Theoretical Domains Framework to "identified relevant psychosocial drivers of the behaviour". Intervention functions of education, training and modelling were selected via COM-B mapping. The approach underpinned the intervention's content development for prescribing behaviour change.
requirements: A behavioural diagnosis identifying what needs to change
Mapping of intervention functions using the COM-B
examples: The intervention functions, 'education', 'training' and 'modelling' were identified as the most appropriate for changing AMR prescribing behaviour

Theory-based electronic learning intervention to support appropriate antibiotic prescribing by nurse and pharmacist independent prescribers: an acceptability and feasibility experimental study using mixed methods.
